title: QUIC RFC 9000 Stream Priority Runtime Architecture
purpose: Describe the bounded runtime path that stores a local stream priority on each writable stream and uses that priority to order queued application sends without introducing any on-wire prioritization exchange.
design_summary: Each writable stream owns a local priority value in stream bookkeeping, and the public QuicStream facade exposes that value as a simple local-only property. The runtime snapshots the current priority when it queues delayed application sends, then flushes queued writes in descending priority order with FIFO tie-breaking for equal priorities. The priority never changes the wire format, does not introduce a built-in priority exchange, and does not alter the existing stream frame codec or transport-parameter surfaces. A small permanent benchmark suite exercises the exact queue-ordering comparator so the delayed-send hot path remains visible in the repo's performance evidence.
data_and_state_considerations: The priority value is runtime-local state. It is not serialized, persisted, or advertised to the peer. A write that has already been queued keeps the priority snapshot captured at queue time; later priority changes affect subsequent writes only. Equal-priority queued writes preserve their original enqueue order so the runtime remains stable under repeated writes.
edge_cases_and_constraints: Setting priority on a stream without a writable side should fail rather than pretending to affect scheduling.
Priority must not introduce any new on-wire exchange or frame type.
Queued application sends must preserve FIFO order when priorities are equal.
Already-protected packets are not preempted by a later priority change.
The local priority model remains separate from candidate-path, multipath, and HTTP/3 priority behavior.
alternatives_considered: Add a wire-level priority exchange; rejected because the requirement set explicitly says QUIC must not provide a built-in prioritization exchange.
Use a single connection-wide priority instead of a per-stream value; rejected because the requirement set asks for application-visible stream controls and per-stream resource allocation.
Defer all priority handling to a higher protocol layer; rejected because the current runtime already owns the write queue that can honor a local stream priority without any protocol change.
risks: A local snapshot taken at queue time means priority changes do not reorder bytes already waiting to flush.
Sorting queued sends adds a small amount of work on the delayed-write path.
The slice should not be mistaken for HTTP/3 or wire-level prioritization support.

supplemental_sections.heading: Scope
supplemental_sections.content: This design covers only local stream-priority storage and priority-aware ordering of queued application sends on the active runtime. It does not claim transport-parameter negotiation, wire-level priority exchange, HTTP/3 dependency trees, multipath scheduling, or candidate-path selection.
